summary:
Today's deforestation monitoring relies heavily on C-band radar, which typically flags forest loss only once the trees are already gone. We wanted to find out what C-band misses.

Our map runs the same detection method on C-band data (Sentinel-1) and on the NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band data, then compares the two. Wherever only the L-band registers a change, the pixel turns orange. Those pixels are the blind spot in current monitoring, and they account for 98.6% of all L-band detections.

For the Dancing with SARs challenge, we worked in Paragominas, Brazil, a well-studied selective-logging hotspot. We used NISAR GCOV data from the ASF DAAC (10 scenes, Jun–Oct 2026) with Sentinel-1 as the C-band baseline (9 scenes). In dense tropical forest, L-band reaches more than 10 m into the canopy while C-band only sees the top 1–2 m, and our results confirm it: NISAR detected 331,922 pixels of change that C-band caught in only 16,467.

This is the first application of operational NISAR data, which became publicly available just 8 days before this challenge.

Forest managers, conservation agencies, carbon-offset verifiers, and researchers can use this to catch degradation earlier, before it becomes full deforestation.
details:
map that quantifies the "blind spot" in current deforestation monitoring, the areas where C-band radar (Sentinel-1) fails to detect early-stage forest change that NISAR L-band radar does catch.

The method is multi-temporal backscatter differencing: for each pixel, we subtract the first scene's backscatter from the last scene's backscatter over a 4-month window. Pixels where the drop exceeds a threshold (−6 dB for L-band, −4 dB for C-band) are flagged as change. We run this independently on NISAR L-band HV (10 scenes, Jun 24 – Oct 22, 2026) and Sentinel-1 C-band VH (9 scenes, Jun 19 – Sep 30, 2026) over the same 55 × 55 km area in Paragominas, Pará, Brazil. The "blind spot" layer is the set of pixels where L-band fires an alert but C-band does not.

The result: 98.6% of L-band detections (327,434 of 331,922 pixels) are invisible to C-band.

What benefits does it have?

  • It makes the NISAR value proposition concrete and visible. Rather than stating "L-band is more sensitive," the map shows exactly where and how much C-band misses.
  • It works with data that became publicly available 8 days before the challenge. No calibration, no preprocessing beyond clipping, the pipeline is reproducible by anyone with a laptop and a free Earthdata account.
  • The method is sensor-agnostic: the same differencing logic applies to any multi-temporal SAR stack, so it generalizes to future NISAR data, ALOS-4, or any L-band mission.

What is the intended impact?

Forest monitoring agencies (INPE/DETER in Brazil, GFW globally) currently rely on C-band and optical systems that detect clear-cutting but miss selective logging and canopy thinning, the Stage 1 degradation that precedes irreversible loss by weeks to months. This project provides a template for integrating NISAR into operational early-warning pipelines: once full L-band data is available, the same pipeline can run at national scale and feed into alert systems as a complementary layer.

What tools, languages, and software did you useHow is the project creative?

  1. First operational NISAR application. Every prior study on L-band vs C-band for early deforestation used ALOS PALSAR-2 (decommissioned 2024) or research-grade data. This is the first time publicly available NISAR operational data has been ingested, processed, and used for change detection.
  2. The blind-spot layer as a visualization. Prior work reports accuracy tables (e.g., "L-band: 67% vs C-band: 34%"). We instead produce a map layer, a spatial artifact a forest manager can open and point at: "this is what you're missing." The orange pixels are the argument.

What factors did the team consider?

  • Study area selection: Paragominas was chosen because it is a well-documented selective-logging hotspot (Watanabe 2018; Flores-Anderson 2025; Reiche 2025), has flat Amazonian terrain (minimizing SAR layover/shadow artifacts), and is covered by INPE's DETER alert system for future validation.
  • Polarization: We used HV (cross-polarized) for NISAR because it is most sensitive to canopy structure change. For Sentinel-1, VH is the only available channel in dual-pol GRD products; HV ≈ VH by reciprocity, so the comparison is valid.
  • Threshold selection: We tuned the dB threshold by inspecting the distribution of change values. −6 dB for L-band captures genuine structural drops while excluding seasonal noise (June = dry, October = wet). −4 dB for C-band accounts for its lower signal-to-noise ratio.
  • Data maturity: NISAR Provisional data (calibrated but not yet validated) was used to maximize temporal coverage (10 scenes vs 3 if restricted to Validated only). This is acceptable for a proof-of-concept.
  • Scope trade-off: We prioritized a clean, defensible single-AOI result over a multi-region or multi-method approach. The 48-hour window made this the right call: one area, two sensors, one clear number.
dataRefs: NASA-ISRO NISAR and Sentinel-1 ESA via ASF DAAC
